title: Brief of respondent Ricky D. Dixon, Secretary, Florida Department of Corrections in opposition

No. 25-580

IN THE
Supreme Court of the United States
_______________
GARY RICHARD WHITTON,
Petitioner,
v.
SECRETARY, FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS,
Respondent.
_______________
On Petition For A Writ Of Certiorari To The
U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
_______________
BRIEF IN OPPOSITION
_______________




OFFICE OF THE
  ATTORNEY GENERAL
State of Florida
The Capitol – PL-01
Tallahassee, FL
  32399-1050
Phone: (850) 414-3300
jeffrey.desousa @
  myfloridalegal.com
JAMES UTHMEIER
Attorney General of
Florida

JEFFREY PAUL DESOUSA
Acting Solicitor General
  Counsel of Record
CHRISTOPHER J. BAUM
Senior Deputy Solicitor
General
Counsel for Respondent

i


CAPITAL CASE
QUESTION PRESENTED
Petitioner was convicted of capital murder, and the
Florida state courts rejected his habeas claims. On
federal habeas review, petitioner raised a new claim
under Giglio, asserting that a witness testified falsely
about his arrest record. The state courts were never
presented with and never passed on that claim.
Instead, the Florida Supreme Court rejected
petitioner’s other claims and held that the evidence
against petiti oner was “overwhelming.” In so doing,
the Florida Supreme Court never mentioned or relied
on newly discovered inculpatory DNA evidence
against petitioner.
In assessing petitioner’s newly raised federal
habeas claim, the Eleventh Circuit held that the
Florida Supreme Court’s finding of “overwhelming
evidence” amounted to a holding that the jury would
have reached the same result. After reviewing the
evidence against petitioner, the Eleventh Circuit
concluded that the Florida Supreme Court’s finding
was not unreasonable , and thus that it was owed
deference under AEDPA. In so doing, the Eleventh
Circuit also mentioned the newly discovered
inculpatory DNA evidence.
The question  presented is whether the  Eleventh
Circuit was correct that the Florida Supreme Court’s
finding of overwhelming evidence against petitioner
was reasonable under AEDPA’s deferential standard
of review.

1


STATEMENT
1.  The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty
Act of 1996 (AEDPA) limits the role of federal courts
in reviewing state criminal convictions. A federal
court shall not grant habeas relief unless “the
applicant has exhausted the remedies available in the
courts of the State,” subject to exceptions not at issue
here. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1)(A); see Ex parte Royall ,
117 U.S. 241 (1886).
Beyond exhaustion, a  federal court “shall not”
grant habeas relief on a “claim that was adjudicated
on the merits in State court proceedings” unless the
State decision (1) “was contrary to, or involved an
unreasonable application of, clearly established
Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court of
the United States”  or (2) “was based on an
unreasonable determination of the facts in light of the
evidence presented.” 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d); see Williams
v. Taylor, 529 U.S. 362 (2000).
As to Section 2254(d)(1), a “state court  decision is
contrary to clearly established federal law if the state
court either arrives at a conclusion opposite to  that
reached by the Supreme Court on a question of law or
decides a case differently than the Supreme Court has
on a set of materially indistinguishable facts.” Davis
v. Sellers , 940 F.3d 1175, 1185 (11th Cir. 2019)
(cleaned up).  The “state court’s ruling” must be “so
lacking in justification that there was an error well
understood and comprehended in existing law beyond
any possibility for fairminded disagreement.”
Harrington v. Richter, 562 U.S. 86, 103 (2011).

2


As to § 2254(d)(2), federal courts must “accord the
state trial court substantial deference” to its factual
determinations. Brumfield v. Cain, 576 U.S. 305, 314
(2015); see Wilson v. Sellers, 584 U.S. 122, 125 (2018)
(courts must review “the specific reasons given by the
state court and defe [r] to  those reasons if they are
reasonable”). Federal courts cannot grant relief “even
if some of the state court’s individual factual findings
were erroneous—so long as the decision, taken as a
whole, doesn’t constitute an unreasonable
determination of the facts and isn’t based on any such
determination.” Pye v. Warden, Ga. Diagnostic Prison,
50 F.4th 1025, 1035 (11th Cir. 2022)  (quotation
omitted). And “a  determination of a factual issue
made by a State court  shall be presumed to be
correct,” rebuttable by a  petitioner only upon “clear
and convincing evidence.” 28  U.S.C. §  2254(e)(1).
These standards require federal courts to give the
“benefit of the doubt” to merits decisions issued by the
courts of the  sovereign States. Woodford v. Visciotti ,
537 U.S. 19, 24 (2002) (per curiam).
2.  James Maulden was found stabbed to death in
his room at the Sun and Sand Motel in Destin,
Florida, on October 10, 1990. Pet. App. 3a. Along with
a skull fracture, he had sustained three fatal stab
wounds to the chest and other stab wounds on his
body. Id. The motel room was covered in blood spatter,
consistent with “significant bleeding” and “violent
combat.” Id.
According to a motel clerk, Maulden had checked
in the day before after arriving in another man’s car.
Id. That man had helped Maulden check in, as
Maulden was intoxicated. Id. After doing so, the man

3


left; the clerk, however, saw someone get into the
man’s car, parked near Maulden’s room, later that
night, and gave police the car’s license -plate number.
Id. That led police to petitioner Gary Richard Whitton.
Id.
At the police station, petitioner told the officers
that he knew Maulden from rehab and acknowledged
that he had dropped Maulden off at the motel the
previous afternoon. Pet. App. 4a. After denying that
he had gone back to the motel later, petitioner
admitted that he had returned to Maulden’s room,
discovered him dead, and fled in a panic. Id.
Petitioner’s fingerprints were found on a bag near
Maulden’s body. Id.
Police found “medium velocity” blood “spatter”
consistent with “a stabbing or a beating,” targeted by
“forceful bloodshed,” inside of petitioner’s boots. Id.;
see Pet. 9. The blood spatter traveled “from top to
bottom” inside the boots, belying petitioner’s claim
that blood from the motel seeped into his socks from
“between his boot soles” and “uppers.” Pet. App. 4a.
The blood stains matched Maulden’s blood type, as did
blood stains in petitioner’s car. Id.
3.  At trial, the State offered evidence that the day
before Maulden was found dead, Maulden had asked
petitioner to drive him to Maulden’s bank. Pet. App.
5a. Maulden, intoxicated, withdrew his account
balance of $1,135.88. Id. When the two arrived at the
motel, petitioner wrote down a false license -plate
number on the registration, but the clerk noticed and
corrected it. Id. The next day, petitioner bought gas at
2:37 a.m., paid his car registration fee, and paid two
utility bills, totaling about $228. Pet. App. 5a, 40a.

4


The State also called two witnesses, Jake Ozio and
Kenneth McCullough, who were incarcerated with
petitioner. Pet. App. 5a. Both testified that petitioner
confessed to the murder. Id. Ozio had been arrested
for burglary and possession of a short-barrel shotgun,
but shortly before petitioner’s trial he was released on
probation and his firearm charge was reduced to a
misdemeanor. Id. He testified at trial that he had
overheard petitioner tell McCullough that he had
“stabbed the bastard.” Id. McCullough, who was
serving a 15 -year sentence for seven felony
convictions, corroborated Ozio’s account. Id. He also
admitted that he was a “close personal friend” of the
prosecutor’s mother. Pet. App. 6a.
Petitioner testified in his own defense, claiming
that he had returned to the motel to tell Maulden that
his mother was looking for him and that he fled after
he found Maulden dead. Id. He added that a former
tenant had recently given him $200 to pay off utility
bills. Id.
The defense also called a DNA analyst from the
Florida Department of Law Enforcement, who
testified that although the blood on petitioner’s boots
was Maulden’s blood type, the DNA matched neither
petitioner’s nor Maulden’s DNA.1 Id.

1 In 2002, the State retested the blood on petitioner’s boots
and determined that the inside of the right boot contained blood
from “a mixture of two or more individuals” with the “major
donor” matching “the DNA profile of James Maulden.” Pet. App.
6a n.5. The State also determined that Maulden was a DNA
contributor to one area on the left boot and a possible contributor
to another area on the right boot. Id.

5


The jury found petitioner guilty of murder and
robbery. Pet. App. 7a.
At the penalty phase, the advisory jury
unanimously recommended a death sentence. Id.
After finding five aggravating circumstances and
several non -statutory mitigating factors, the
sentencing court imposed the death penalty. Pet. App.
7a–8a.2 The Florida Supreme Court affirmed on direct
appeal. Pet. App. 8a.
4.  In 1997, petitioner filed for state postconviction
relief. Pet. App. 10a. As relevant here, petitioner
claimed that because Ozio allegedly recanted his trial
testimony that petitioner confessed to him in prison ,
the State violated his rights under Giglio v. United
States, 405 U.S. 150 (1972) . Pet. App. 11a. The state
postconviction court denied relief on all of petitioner’s
claims, and the Florida Supreme Court affirmed. Pet.
App. 12a.
As for petitioner’s Giglio claim, the Florida
Supreme Court found that petitioner “failed to
present any evidence in support of his claim.” Pet.
App. 131a. He “failed to demonstrate that” Ozio’s
testimony “was false” because “Ozio refused to testify
[in the postconviction proceedings] and [petitioner]
did not seek to have Ozio’s affidavit submitted into
evidence.” Id. And “even if Ozio’s trial testimony was

2 The five aggravators were: (1) petitioner murdered
Maulden while on parole for an armed robbery; (2) petitioner was
previously convicted of another felony involving the use or threat
of violence; (3) the crime was committed to avoid arrest; (4) the
crime was committed for pecuniary gain; and (5) the crime was
heinous, atrocious, or cruel. Whitton v. State, 649 So. 2d 861, 864
(Fla. 1994).

6


false, [petitioner] ha[d] not demonstrated that the
State was aware that Ozio intended to present false
testimony.” Id.
Petitioner did not claim in state court—as he does
now—that the State violated his Giglio rights by
allowing Ozio’s false testimony regarding his arrest
record to go uncorrected. As a result, the Florida
Supreme Court did not address this new claim.
In the course of rejecting petitioner’s other claims,
the Florida Supreme Court held that petitioner’s
appellate counsel did not perform deficiently and that
petitioner could not establish prejudice given the
“overwhelming evidence against” him. Pet. App. 153a.
After a successive state habeas petition based on
Hurst v. Florida , 577 U.S. 92 (2016)  was rejected,
petitioner sought federal habeas relief. Pet. App. 12a.
5.  In petitioner’s federal habeas petition, he again
pressed his Giglio claim regarding Ozio’s testimony.
Pet. App. 13a. But he added a new claim: That Ozio
testified he had “never previously been arrested”
(before his most recent arrest).  Pet. App. 79a. Ozio
had a juvenile record, and the State’s files included
this information. Id. After holding an evidentiary
hearing, the district court found that this did not give
rise to a Giglio violation because, in its view, a
juvenile arrest “ordinarily would not be admissible to
impeach a witness” and thus the false testimony
“could not have made a difference.” Id. The district
court denied habeas relief on all of petitioner’s claims,
but granted a certificate of appealability as to a few
issues, including petitioner’s Giglio claim regarding
Ozio’s false testimony. Pet. App. 121a.

7


On appeal, the Eleventh Circuit concluded that
(1) Ozio’s testimony about his arrest record was false;
(2) the State had those records; and (3)  the State
“capitalized on the false testimony by portraying Ozio
as a young kid with no criminal past.” Pet. App. 34a–
35a. The State argued that petitioner failed to exhaust
this claim in state court, but the Eleventh Circuit
declined to address that argument because it
concluded that petitioner’s claim failed on the merits.
Pet. App. 35a n.10. The Eleventh Circuit rejected the
district court’s conclusion that the Giglio violation
would not have made a difference, explaining that the
impeachment evidence likely would have been
admissible and that Ozio’s juvenile record would have
undermined his credibility. Pet. App. 35 –36a. As a
result, the Eleventh Circuit could not “affirm the
district court’s decision on its finding of harmless
error.” Pet. App. 36a.
The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the rejection of
petitioner’s claim, however, on the other basis
advanced by the State: That under AEDPA, the court
“owe[d] deference to the Florida Supreme Court’s
determination that, even without [petitioner’s]
confession, the State marshalled overwhelming
evidence that would have caused the jury to reach the
same result.” Pet. App. 37a.  In reaching that
conclusion, the Eleventh Circuit examined the
voluminous evidence considered by the Florida
Supreme Court. Pet. App. 40a–42a. It also noted that
after retesting the DNA, the State confirmed that the
inside of petitioner’s boot contained blood matching
the victim’s DNA profile. Pet. App. 42a.
 Petitioner now seeks this Court’s review.

8


REASONS FOR DENYING THE PETITION
Petitioner contended, for the first time on federal
habeas review, that the State violated his rights
under Giglio v. United States, 405 U.S. 150 (1972), by
failing to correct a witness’s false statement at trial
that he had never been arrested before. Petitioner
never presented this claim in Florida state court and
therefore the Florida Supreme Court never considered
it when concluding that petitioner was not entitled to
habeas relief. Nor did he present any evidentiary
basis for that claim to the Florida state courts.
In reviewing the Florida Supreme Court’s decision
under Section 2254, the Eleventh Circuit declined to
reach whether petitioner had exhausted this new
claim (or whether he was entitled to develop it
factually for the first time in federal court) and
instead rejected it on the merits. The Eleventh Circuit
held that even assuming that petitioner established a
Giglio violation based on that testimony, he was not
entitled to federal habeas relief because the Florida
Supreme Court reasonably determined that
overwhelming evidence supported the guilty verdict.
That determination, the Eleventh Circuit explained,
was an implicit holding that the (unexhausted) Giglio
violation would not have been prejudicial. Under
AEDPA, the Eleventh Circuit was bound to defer to
the Florida Supreme Court’s finding of overwhelming
evidence unless it was “so obviously wrong that its
error lies beyond any possibility for fairminded
disagreement.” Shinn v.  Kayer, 592 U.S. 111, 118
(2020).
After reviewing the evidence canvassed by the
Florida Supreme Court—evidence that did not include

9


the retested DNA—the Eleventh Circuit held that the
Florida Supreme Court’s prejudice determination was
reasonable. In so doing, the Eleventh Circuit also
mentioned that the retested DNA evidence  helped
support its own conclusion that the Florida Supreme
Court’s decision was reasonable.
Whether or not the Eleventh Circuit’s reliance on
the retested DNA was proper, its  holding does not
conflict with any decision, cited by petitioner or
otherwise. Instead, the cases cited by  petitioner hold
that when assessing prejudice for Brady-type errors,
courts may not rely on evidence that the jury never
saw. But the Florida Supreme Court relied only on
evidence that the jury saw, and the Eleventh Circuit
held only that the Florida Supreme Court’s implicit
lack-of-prejudice decision was reasonable, not that the
Giglio error was harmless  because of evidence not
before the jury.
In any event, the decision below was correct. Even
setting aside the retested DNA evidence, the Eleventh
Circuit reviewed the evidence that the jury did see
and correctly concluded that the Florida Supreme
Court’s finding of overwhelming evidence against
petitioner was not so obviously wrong as to be beyond
fairminded disagreement. Although petitioner strains
to suggest that the retested DNA evidence was critical
to that analysis, reading the Eleventh Circuit’s
decision and the evidence it relied on rebuts that
notion.
Certiorari is also unwarranted because the
question presented (as framed by petitioner) was not
briefed, argued, or analyzed below. In other words, the
Eleventh Circuit never considered whether it was

10


proper to rely on the retested DNA evidence  in
applying AEDPA deference . And the centerpiece of
petitioner’s claim for relief—the Giglio claim based on
the false arrest -record testimony —was never
exhausted or factually developed in state court.
Striking the portion of the Eleventh Circuit’s opinion
discussing the retested DNA evidence thus could not
result in petitioner receiving federal habeas relief.  It
would instead amount to mere opinion revision.
The petition should be denied.
I. THIS CASE DOES NOT IMPLICATE ANY CIRCUIT
SPLIT.
Petitioner argues that the Eleventh Circuit’s
decision created a conflict with other circuits and a
state court of last resort. It did not. Instead,
petitioner’s asserted conflict is based on a holding that
the Eleventh Circuit never issued.
Petitioner’s sole remaining claim is  a Giglio claim
based on Ozio’s false testimony regarding his arrest
record. To prove that claim on direct review, petitioner
must have shown “(1)  the prosecutor knowingly used
perjured testimony or  failed to correct what he
subsequently learned was false  testimony; and (2)
such use was material i.e., that there is  any
reasonable likelihood that the false testimony could
have affected the judgment.” United States v.  Stein,
846 F.3d 1135, 1147 (11th Cir. 2017)  (quotation
omitted). Under Chapman v. California , before a
Giglio error “can be held harmless, the court must be
able to declare a belief that it was harmless beyond a
reasonable doubt.” 386 U.S. 18, 24 (1967). Petitioner
did not raise a Giglio claim based on Ozio’s false

11


arrest-record testimony either on direct review or
state collateral review, however.
“[I]n order to obtain federal habeas relief, a state
prisoner must ‘show far more’ than ‘clear error.’” Klein
v. Martin, 607 U.S. ___, 2026 WL 189976, at *4 (2026)
(per curiam) (quoting Shinn, 592 U.S. at 118).
Petitioner must have established that the Giglio error
“resulted in actual prejudice.” Brecht v. Abrahamson,
507 U.S. 619, 637 (1993) (quotation omitted). “Under
this test, relief is proper only if the federal court has
grave doubt about whether a trial error of federal law
had substantial and injurious effect or influence in
determining the jury ’s verdict.” Davis v. Ayala , 576
U.S. 257, 267–68 (2015) (quotations omitted). Put
another way, “[t] he habeas claimant
must . . . establish that the state court ‘blunder[ed] so
badly that every fairminded jurist would disagree ’
with the decision. ” Klein, 607 U.S. ___, 2026 WL
189976, at *4 (quoting Mays v. Hines , 592 U.S. 385,
392 (2021)). This standard “ reflects the view that a
State is not to be put to th[e] arduous task [of retrying
a defendant] based on mere speculation that the
defendant was prejudiced by trial error; the court
must find that the defendant was actually prejudiced
by the error.” Ayala, 576 U.S. at 268.
Yet even that does not end the matter. The Florida
Supreme Court held that, even setting aside
McCullough’s or Ozio’s testimony regarding
petitioner’s confessions, the evidence against
petitioner was “overwhelming.” Pet. App. 153a. As the
Eleventh Circuit explained, “a lack -of-prejudice
holding immediately follows” from that conclusion
because “errors are harmless ‘under the Brecht

12


standard where  . . . other evidence of guilt is
overwhelming.’” Pet. App. 39a. The Florida Supreme
Court’s implicit Chapman holding, concluding that
any error was harmless, is reviewed under AEDPA.
Ayala, 576 U.S. at 268 –69; see Johnson v. Williams ,
568 U.S. 289, 300 (2013)  (federal courts have “no
authority to impose mandatory opinion -writing
standards on state courts”).
And “[w]hen a Chapman decision is reviewed
under AEDPA, a federal court may not award habeas
relief under §  2254 unless the harmlessness
determination itself  was unreasonable.” Ayala, 576
U.S. at 2 69; see Wilson , 584 U.S. at 125 (AEDPA
requires courts to review “the  specific reasons given
by the state court and defe [r] to those reasons if they
are reasonable”). Petitioner thus bore the burden to
establish that the state court’s decision to reject his
claim “was so lacking in justification that there was
an error well understood and comprehended in
existing law beyond any possibility for fairminded
disagreement.” Ayala, 576 U.S. at 269 –70. As the
Eleventh Circuit correctly held, and as discussed
below, petitioner did not meet that burden.
Petitioner’s claim of conflict on the question of
“whether a court assessing trial prejudice may rely on
evidence the jury never saw,” Pet. 18, is thus illusory.
The Eleventh Circuit was not assessing trial prejudice
when it rejected petitioner’s claim; when it did assess
trial prejudice, it concluded that the Giglio violation
was not harmless. Pet. App. 36a. Nor did the Eleventh
Circuit “h[o]ld that a Giglio violation can be deemed
harmless on the basis of DNA evidence developed a
decade after trial.” Pet.  18. Instead, the Eleventh

13


Circuit held that  even though the error was not
harmless, the Florida Supreme Court’s conclusion
that the evidence against petitioner was
“overwhelming” was reasonable and thus owed
deference under AEDPA , precluding habeas relief. 3
Pet. App. 43a. That fact-bound determination is not
worthy of this Court’s review.
Even the reading of the Eleventh Circuit’s decision
most charitable to petitioner does not give rise to a
conflict. Nothing in the Eleventh Circuit’s decision
purports to give dispositive or outcome-determinative
weight to the retested DNA evidence in assessing the
reasonableness of the Florida Supreme Court’s
decision. For good reason: The Florida Supreme Court
never relied on it or mentioned it . But even if

3 Although the Florida Supreme Court did not purport to
reject petitioner’s exhausted Giglio claims regarding Ozio’s
testimony (not at issue here) on this basis, the Eleventh Circuit
properly concluded that it should not “accept readings of AEDPA
that ‘strictly limit[]’ a state court ‘to the particular justifications’
it ‘memorialized in its writ ten opinion.’” Pet. App. 39a (quoting
Pye v. Warden, Ga. Diagnostic Prison, 50 F.4th 1025, 1039 (11th
Cir. 2022)); see also Klein, 607 U.S. ___ 2026 WL 189976, at *4
(“a federal court must ‘carefully consider all the reasons and
evidence supporting the state court’s decision ’” (quoting Mays,
592 U.S. at 391)); Blankenship v. Hall, 542 F.3d 1253, 1272 (11th
Cir. 2008)  (explaining “implicit findings of fact are entitled to
deference under § 2254(d) to the same extent as explicit findings
of fact”).  The Florida Supreme Court expressly concluded that
the evidence against petitioner was “overwhelming” even
without the testimony regarding his confessions. Pet. App. 153a.
And “a lack-of-prejudice holding immediately follows” from that
conclusion. Pet. App. 39a. See Miller-El v. Cockrell, 537 U.S. 322,
347 (2003)  (A state court “need not make detailed findings
addressing all the evidence before it.” ). Under AEDPA, the
Eleventh Circuit owed that conclusion deference.

14


petitioner could show that the Eleventh Circuit could
not have concluded that the Florida Supreme Court
reasonably determined that the evidence was
“overwhelming” without the DNA evidence, the
Eleventh Circuit’s reliance on that evidence in this
context does not give rise to a circuit split.
In Apanovitch v. Bobby , the Sixth Circuit
explained that the results of a recent DNA test were
irrelevant to the analysis of whether a Brady error
was prejudicial. 648 F.3d 434, 437 (6th Cir. 2011). And
in State v. Best, the North Carolina Supreme Court
likewise concluded that later -developed DNA
evidence was irrelevant to the Brady prejudice
analysis. 852 S.E.2d 191, 198 n.4 (N.C. 2020). Neither
case addressed whether it was permissible to consider
later-developed DNA evidence in assessing the
distinct question of whether a state court’s decision
was reasonable under AEDPA.
In determining that the evidence against
petitioner here was “overwhelming” (therefore
precluding a finding a prejudice) , moreover, the
Florida Supreme Court did not rely on or even
mention the retested DNA evidence. And the Eleventh
Circuit’s holding rejecting petitioner’s habeas claim
was limited to a determination that the Florida
Supreme Court’s decision was reasonable under
AEDPA. Pet. App. 43a. That holding does not conflict
with either the Sixth Circuit’s holding or the North
Carolina Supreme Court’s holding that evidence not
available at trial is irrelevant to the prejudice inquiry
under Brady (which is distinct from the inquiry under
AEDPA).

15


The conflict analysis with Browning v. Trammell,
717 F.3d 1092 (10th Cir. 2013) , is similar. There, the
Tenth Circuit concluded that only Brady evidence
available before trial was relevant  to the Brady
materiality analysis . Id. at 1104 . But the ultimate
question answered by the Eleventh Circuit here was
not whether petitioner established a Giglio
violation—the Eleventh Circuit held that he had
because the testimony was not harmless (Pet. App.
36a)—but whether the Florida Supreme Court
reasonably determined that “ Ozio’s testimony,
overall, was immaterial to the jury’s verdict ” ( Pet.
App. 36a) because the evidence against petitioner was
overwhelming (Pet. App. 37a). In other words, in
determining that the Giglio violation was not
harmless (like the Trammell court determined that
the Brady violation was material), the Eleventh
Circuit did not consider any evidence not available at
trial. It did so only when considering the distinct
question of whether the Florida Supreme Court’s
finding of overwhelming evidence against petit ioner
was reasonable, precluding relief despite any knowing
use of false testimony . The Trammell court simply
never confronted the question of whether that would
have been proper under AEDPA because the state
court there had made no overwhelming-evidence
finding.
The Second Circuit’s decision in United States v.
Jean-Baptiste, 166 F.3d 102 (2d Cir. 1999) , is even
farther afield. There, the court held that a conviction
could not be upheld on direct appeal based on evidence
contained in an affidavit proffered during the appeal.
Id. at 108 . That a conviction can be sustained only

16


based on evidence presented to the jury has no bearing
on the AEDPA-deference question here.
Even petitioner characterizes the cases supporting
his purported conflict as “draw[ing] the same bright
line: when a court evaluates prejudice, it must confine
itself to the record that was before the jury.” Pet. 19.
That is what the Florida Supreme Court did. And the
Eleventh Circuit itself concluded that the Giglio
violation was not harmless  based only on the record
before the jury . Pet. App. 36a. But the Eleventh
Circuit did not reject petitioner’s claim on that basis ;
it held that  the Florida Supreme Co urt’s lack-ofprejudice evaluation —itself confined to the record
before the jury —was reasonable under AEDPA’s
deferential standard. Pet. App. 43a. No conflict exists.
At bottom, petitioner’s asserted conflict rests on
the proposition that the Eleventh Circuit denied
habeas relief because it held that petitioner was not
prejudiced by any knowing use of false testimony .
E.g., Pet. 30–31 (“The Eleventh Circuit expressly held
that it could rely on post-trial evidence . . . to conclude
that an unconstitutional  use of false testimony was
‘harmless.’”). That proposition  is wrong  even on the
face of the Eleventh Circuit’s opinion . Pet. App. 36a
(“[W]e cannot affirm the district court’s decision on its
finding of harmless error.”). The petition either elides
or ignores the standard of review under AEDPA
applied by the Eleventh Circuit: whether the Florida
Supreme Court’s decision was  “so obviously wrong
that its error lies beyond any possibility for
fairminded disagreement.” Pye, 50 F.4th at 1041 –42
(quoting Shinn, 592 U.S. at 118); see also Harrington,
562 U.S. at 101. In other words, the question

17


answered by the Eleventh Circuit was not whether the
Giglio error “had a prejudicial effect on the outcome of
a trial”; it was whether the Florida Supreme Court
reasonably determined as much under AEDPA’s
deferential standard.  Pet. App. 43a.  And it did —
without relying on any evidence not before the jury.
Last, even if any tension existed between the
decision below and the decisions on which petitioner
relies, the Eleventh Circuit’s decision is unpublished.
In the Eleventh Circuit, “unpublished decisions are
not binding authority and they are persuasive only to
the extent that a subsequent panel finds the rationale
expressed in that opinion to be persuasive after an
independent consideration of the legal issue.” Koletas
v. United States, 159 F.4th 813, 820 (11th Cir. 2025)
(quotation omitted).4 Petitioner thus cannot establish
any conflict worthy of this Court’s review —let alone
on an y issue that petitioner actually exhausted in
state court, see infra at 21.
II. THE DECISION BELOW WAS CORRECT.
The Eleventh Circuit’s decision to de fer to the
Florida Supreme Court’s rejection of petitioner’s
Giglio claim was mandated by AEDPA: The Florida
Supreme Court’s holding that the evidence of
petitioner’s guilt was “overwhelming” was manifestly
reasonable. In determining that the Florida Supreme
Court’s decision —which did not rely on or even
mention the retested DNA evidence—was reasonable,
the Eleventh Circuit relied on the following facts:

4 Petitioner thus errs in suggesting that the Eleventh Circuit’s drive-by
reliance on the new DNA evidence will “govern every habeas proceeding
in that circuit,” Pet. 31.

18


• “The undisputed facts place[d] [petitioner] at
the scene of the crime the night that Maulden
was killed,” Pet. App. 40a;
• “[T]he motel clerk saw [petitioner’s] car parked
at the motel, and [petitioner] admitted he was
at the motel,” id.;
• Petitioner’s “boots and his car were stained
with blood,” id.;
• That blood, “after later retesting, matched
Maulden’s DNA,”; id.;
• “[T]he blood stains on and inside [petitioner’s]
boots are consistent with ‘a stabbing or a
beating,’” id.;
• Petitioner “could not explain the downward
blood spatter on the inside of his boots,” id.; and
• Petitioner’s “car contained a power and gas
receipt and a car wash ticket for 2:37
a.m. . . . the night of the murder, id.
Even setting aside one piece of evidence that the
Eleventh Circuit considered —the retested DNA that
later matched Maulden’s DNA —the evidence was
indeed “overwhelming.” As the Eleventh Circuit
explained, petitioner “can’t rebut the State’s blood -
spatter evidence.” Pet. App. 41a. The inside of
petitioner’s boots contained blood matching
Maulden’s blood type and were the “‘target for forceful
bloodshed’ and ‘medium velocity’ blood spatter
consistent with a “stabbing or a beating.’” Id. The
evidence also suggested that “the blood traveled from
the top of [petitioner’s] boots to the bottom, directly
contradicting [his] testimony that he was in
Maulden’s room for only a minute before fleeing.” Id.
And “the State’s expert rebutted [petitioner’s] theory
that blood seeped into his boots through their bottoms

19


by testifying that some of the downward blood spatter
had dried before [petitioner] put his boots back on;
[petitioner] could not have been wearing his boots
when ‘the blood spatter occurred on the interior of
them.’” Id. at 41a –42a. Whether or not the DNA
matched Maulden, the blood spatter evidence was
consistent only with petitioner’s guilt. The State also
“introduced expert testimony that effective washing
can eliminate traces of blood” that might logically
have appeared elsewhere on petitioner’s clothin g and
evidence that petitioner “attempted to wash away the
blood he collected in Maulden’s room.” Pet. App. 42a.
After concluding that petitioner “can’t rebut the
State’s blood -spatter evidence,” and rejecting
petitioner’s counterarguments, Pet. App. 41a–42a, the
Eleventh Circuit mentioned that retesting of the DNA
on petitioner’s boots confirmed that the inside of the
boots contained blood with Maulden’s DNA, Pet. App.
42a. But even without the DNA evidence , the court
concluded that the blood spatter evidence “has no
explanation other than one that is consistent with the
defendant’s guilt .” Pet. App. 42a. The blood s patter
was consistent with “a stabbing or a beating”; it
“traveled from the top of [petitioner’s] boots to the
bottom”; and petitioner “could not have been wearing”
the boots “when the blood spatter occurred on the
interior of them.” Pet. App. 41a–42a.
The Eleventh Circuit’s discussion of all this
evidence makes clear that , even before it considered
the retested DNA evidence, it viewed the evidence as
overwhelming—or, at the very least, that the Florida
Supreme Court was not “so obviously wrong” to
conclude that it was. See id. Petitioner is thus simply

20


incorrect in stating  that the Eleventh Circuit
determined that the Florida Supreme Court’s holding
was reasonable based “almost entirely on the basis of”
the DNA evidence, Pet. i, or that it treated the
retested DNA as “dispositive proof,” Pet. 20, or
“outcome-determinative, Pet. 31. Even without the
retested DNA evidence, the “call” was at least
“debatable,” and therefore well within the realm of
fairminded disagreement. Pet. App. 42a.
That the call was debatable is buttressed by
McCullough’s unrebutted testimony that petitioner
confessed to killing Maulden. The Florida Supreme
Court concluded that “ the only evidence that
McCollough may have wanted to recant his trial
testimony” that petitioner confessed  “was hearsay
evidence presented by a third party .” Pet. App. 130a.
The Florida Supreme Court noted that “recantations
are not credible.” Pet. App. 153a. It also expressly held
that the evidence against petitioner was
“overwhelming,” even without the testimony about his
confession. Id. Add in the unrebutted testimony about
the confession , and the Florida Supreme Court’s
determination of overwhelming evidence  was
eminently reasonable.
In sum, petitioner’s repeated assertions that the
Eleventh Circuit’s “reliance on that later -developed
[DNA] evidence was outcome-determinative” (Pet. 31)
are incorrect. Nothing supports petitioner’s ipse dixit
that, without considering that evidence, the Eleventh
Circuit would have held that the Eleventh Circuit
would have found t hat the Florida Supreme Court’s
“overwhelming evidence” determination —made

21


without reliance on the DNA evidence —was
unreasonable.
Next, Petitioner attempts to cast the Florida
Supreme Court’s denial of habeas relief as
unreasonable based on Ozio’s testimony that he had
“never been arrested before.” Pet. 26 –28. That
attempt runs into two insurmountable obstacles.
First, petitioner did not exhaust his Giglio claim
regarding Ozio’s testimony about his arrest record in
state court, and the Florida Supreme Court never had
an opportunity to consider it . See 28 U.S.C.
§ 2254(b)(1)(A) (requiring exhaustion); Ex parte
Royall, 117 U.S. 241  (1886). Petitioner never raised
the arrest-record claim in his state habeas petition or
before any Florida state courts. See Petition, Whitton
v. State of Florida, No. SC12-2522, 2012 WL 9502913
(Fla. Dec. 5, 2012); Whitton v. State , 161 So. 3d 314,
323–24 (Fla. 2014) (assessing only petitioner’s claim
that Ozio falsely testified about petitioner’s
confession). Nor did he develop the factual basis for it
in state court.
The State raised this exhaustion argument below,
see Answer Br., Whitton v. Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of Corrs. ,
No. 23-10786, Dkt. 31, at 55, 72–73 (11th Cir. Feb. 13,
2024), but the Eleventh Circuit declined to address it
because the court resolved the merits of petitioner’s
Giglio claim instead. See Pet. App. 35a n.10. Because
the Florida Supreme Court was never given a chance
to address the arrest -record claim, the Eleventh
Circuit could not have granted habeas relief on that
claim. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1)(A).

22


Second, because the Florida Supreme Court
determined that petitioner’s guilt was supported by
“overwhelming evidence” at trial, petitioner’s
arguments about the prejudicial nature of Ozio’s
testimony that he had “never been arrested before”
(Pet. 26 –28) are beside the point. The Eleventh
Circuit disagreed that the Giglio violation was
harmless here, Pet. App. 36a, but it appropriately
deferred to the Florida Supreme Court’s implicit
conclusion that it was —or would have been had it
been exhausted. “[E]ven if  undisclosed evidence
‘entirely discredit[s]’ a prosecution witness, the failure
to turn over the evidence is not material if
‘considerable’ other evidence ‘link[s]’ the defendant to
the crime and the record provides ‘strong support’ that
the defendant would have been convicted anyway. ”
Klein, 607 U.S. ___, 2026 WL 189976, at *4  (quoting
Strickler v. Green , 527 U.S. 263, 292 –94 (1999)); see
Mansfield v. Sec’y, Dep’t of Corrs., 679 F.3d 1301, 1313
(11th Cir. 2012)  (“[T]he erroneous admission of
evidence is likely to be  harmless under the Brecht
standard where there is significant corroborating
evidence, or where  other evidence of guilt is
overwhelming.” (citations omitted)). Thus, the Florida
Supreme Court’s reasonable determination that the
evidence of guilt was overwhelming constituted a
holding that any Giglio violation (had it been
preserved) would have been harmless.
III. THIS CASE IS A POOR VEHICLE.
For several reasons, this case also does not present
an appropriate vehicle for addressing whether a court
can rely on subsequently tested DNA evidence in this
particular AEDPA context . Petitioner presents the

23


Eleventh Circuit’s consideration of the retested DNA
evidence as a “linchpin” “holding” of its decision. Pet.
18. Reading the relevant portion of the unpublished
opinion, however, clarifies that at most the Eleventh
Circuit considered it to be just one more factor
supporting the reasonableness of the Florida Supreme
Court’s prejudice determination. See Pet. App. 41a –
42a.
In any event, whether it was proper to consider the
retested DNA evidence was not briefed below or
analyzed by the Eleventh Circuit. 5 So the Eleventh
Circuit never assessed , with the aid of adversarial
argument, whether considering that evidence would
be appropriate in applying AEDPA deference. Nor did
it engage with other courts that have held —albeit in
the distinct context of a Brady prejudice
determination—that considering such evidence would
be improper. Instead, it simply considered that
evidence to be  yet another factor supporting the
reasonableness of the Florida Supreme Court’s
decision.
That is why petitioner can assert only that “[t]he
constitutional question”—i.e., his Giglio claim—“was
raised, briefed, and decided at every level,” at least in

5 At most, the parties briefed the question of whether the
retested DNA supported affirming the denial of relief because
“law and justice” did not require  relief under Brown v.
Davenport, 596 U.S. 118, 134 (2022). See Answer Br., Whitton v.
Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of Corrs., No. 23-10786, at 34–35 (11th Cir. Feb.
13, 2024); Reply Br., id., at 23 –24. Neither party discussed
whether the Eleventh Circuit should or could consider it in its
analysis of whether the Florida Supreme Court’s finding of
overwhelming evidence was reasonable under AEDPA.  As a
result, the Eleventh Circuit never analyzed that question.

24


the federal courts. Pet. 31 (emphasis added). (It was
not raised, briefed, or decided at any level in state
court, however, and is thus procedurally barred under
Section 2254(b)(1)(A).) Unlike the Giglio claim, the
question he presents, miscast as it is, was never
briefed in either the district court or in the Eleventh
Circuit. That the issue of considering retested DNA
evidence during the AEDPA deference analysis was
never briefed or even analyzed by the Eleventh
Circuit in this case shows that much more percolation
is needed before this Court’s intervention is
warranted.
Also c ontrary to petitioner’s assertion, if “this
Court holds that prejudice must be measured by the
record before the jury,” Pet. 31,  petitioner would not
be entitled to relief. The Florida Supreme Court never
measured prejudice by anything other than the record
before the jury, and all the Eleventh Circuit held was
that the Florida Supreme Court’s decision survived
AEDPA’s deferential standard of review.
Petitioner, moreover, failed to exhaust his Giglio
claim in state court and thus the Eleventh Circuit
could not grant relief on remand. See supra at 21. So
a decision from this  Court would not “definitively
resolve” this case. Pet. 31. What petitioner seeks is not
to correct a reasoned holding by the Eleventh Circuit
but merely to blue -pencil the court’s opinion by
erasing its tacked-on discussion of the retested DNA
evidence.
What is more, the only evidence supporting
petitioner’s Giglio claim was developed in the federal
evidentiary hearing in the district court. Because it
resolved petitioner’s claim on the merits, however, the

25


Eleventh Circuit did not address the State’s argument
that the district court erred in allowing petitioner to
develop that evidence in the first place because he
“failed to develop the factual basis of [his] claim in
State court proceedings.” 28 U.S.C. § 2254(e)(2); see
Shinn v. Ramirez, 596 U.S. 366, 371 (2022) . Perhaps
because he did not exhaust this Giglio claim in state
court, petitioner did not present any evidence of his
juvenile record in state court and thus failed to
develop the factual basis for that claim. Nor can he
explain why his postconviction counsel could not have
obtained his prior arrest rec ord while litigating in
state court. Even if this Court were to reverse,
petitioner would not be entitled to habeas relief on an
unexhausted claim based on evidence not developed
or presented to the state courts.
CONCLUSION
The petition for a writ of certiorari should be
denied.
